?

FINDING OF FACT

The Veteran's sleep apnea did not have its onset during service and is not causally or etiologically related to any disease, injury, or incident during service.

CONCLUSION OF LAW

The criteria for service connection for sleep apnea are not met.  38 U.S.C. §§ 1131, 5107; 38 C.F.R. § 3.102, 3.303.

REASONS AND BASES FOR FINDING AND CONCLUSION

The Veteran served on active duty from May 1962 to November 1962.

The case is on appeal from a December 2014 rating decision.

In March 2018, the Veteran testified at a Board hearing.

In October 2022, the Board denied service connection for sleep apnea.  The Veteran appealed the Board's denial to the United States Court of Appeal for Veterans Claims (Court) and the parties to this appeal entered an August 2023 Joint Motion for Remand (JMR).  In the JMR, the parties agreed that the denial of service connection sleep apnea should be vacated.  The Court granted the parties' JMR in an Order issued in September 2023.

In November 2023, the Board remanded the claim for additional development.

The Board has limited the discussion below to the relevant evidence required to support its finding of fact and conclusion of law, as well as to the specific contentions regarding the case as raised directly by the Veteran and those reasonably raised by the record.  See Scott v. McDonald, 789 F.3d 1375, 1381 (Fed. Cir. 2015); Robinson v. Peake, 21 Vet. App. 545, 552 (2008).

Service connection for sleep apnea.

Legal Criteria

Service connection may be granted for a disability resulting from a disease or injury incurred in or aggravated by active service.  See 38 U.S.C. § 1131; 38 C.F.R. § 3.303.  A veteran seeking compensation under these provisions must establish three elements: "(1) the existence of a present disability; (2) in-service incurrence or aggravation of a disease or injury; and (3) a causal relationship between the present disability and the disease or injury incurred or aggravated during service."  Saunders v. Wilkie, 886 F.3d 1356, 1361 (Fed. Cir. 2018) (quoting Shedden v. Principi, 381 F.3d 1163, 1167 (Fed. Cir. 2004)).

Analysis

The Veteran contends that he has sleep apnea related to service.  In this regard, he reported in an April 2014 correspondence that he was diagnosed with sleep apnea in 2008 and claimed that it is related to a July 1962 upper respiratory infection.  He then stated in a September 2014 correspondence that an upper respiratory infection he experienced in October 1962 was an exacerbation of the prior infection.

The Veteran's service treatment records (STRs) reflect that he experienced a sore throat, fever, coughing, and shortness of breath in June 1962 and was placed in an upper respiratory infection ward.  The treatment provider reported that a chest x-ray taken at that time did not exhibit the presence of a significant abnormality.  An STR dated a few days later contains a notation of acute upper respiratory disease, treated and cured.  STRs from October 1962 reflect that the Veteran was treated for a cough, cold, and chest pain at such time.  The Veteran completed a report of medical history pursuant to separation from service in October 1962.  He noted having pneumonia as a child, but expressly denied a history of chronic or frequent colds, shortness of breath, pain or pressure in chest, chronic cough, and frequent trouble sleeping.  The Veteran's October 1962 separation examination was marked "normal" for his lungs and chest and did not note any current conditions.  The Veteran completed a report of medical history during reserve service in April 1967.  He reported a few unrelated medical conditions, but expressly denied a history of chronic or frequent colds, shortness of breath, pain or pressure in chest, chronic cough, and frequent trouble sleeping.  During an April 1967 examination, his lungs and chest were marked "normal" and nothing relevant was noted or reported.

The Veteran's post-service private treatment records reflect that he was diagnosed with moderate obstructive sleep apnea in September 2008.  In addition, the Veteran submitted a letter from a private physician in February 2018 that notes the Veteran had a period of hospitalization due to infection during his period of ACDUTRA.  The physician also reports that the Veteran has a septal deviation with nasal obstruction.  The physician stated that the Veteran experienced trauma to his nose during service and that such trauma could have contributed to his septal deviation.

Pursuant to the March 2018 Board remand, the Veteran was afforded an examination for this claim in September 2018.  The Veteran reported injuring his nose during a period of ACDUTRA and that he began using a CPAP machine for sleep apnea in 2001.  The examiner reported that the Veteran was diagnosed with moderate obstructive sleep apnea in 2008 following a sleep study.  The examiner found that it is less likely than not that the Veteran's sleep apnea was incurred in or caused by an in-service injury, event, or illness.  The examiner explained that the Veteran's in-service upper respiratory infection resolved with routine care, he returned to full duty to complete rigorous basic training without residual problems, and he has not suffered from a resulting chronic respiratory condition.  The examiner also explained that the Veteran's septal deviation is a condition distal to the anatomical structures involved in obstructive sleep apnea and is not a risk factor for the condition.  The examiner found that neither the Veteran's long-resolved upper respiratory infection nor his deviated nasal septum contribute to or to cause his obstructive sleep apnea.  The examiner concluded that the Veteran's obstructive sleep apnea is instead caused by a pathophysiologic episodic narrowing of the airway during sleep due to direct mechanical effects on the anatomy of the upper airway.

In the October 2022 decision, the Board denied the claim based on the September 2018 examiner's findings.  However, on appeal, the Court found that the examiner failed to address the Veteran's claims of experiencing breathing problems ever since the in-service upper respiratory infections. 

Pursuant to the November 2023 Board remand, a VA medical opinion for this claim was obtained in November 2023.  The examiner reviewed the Veteran's complete claims file and found that the sleep apnea is less likely than not due to service or the 1962 respiratory infection.  The examiner reported that the Veteran was noted as having moderate retrognathia with a low lying soft palate during an October 2008 examination.  The examiner explained that retrognathia is a condition in which the lower jaw is set further back than the upper jaw.  The examiner also explained that this condition can physically cause disrupted breathing, snoring, and sleep apnea.  The examiner further explained that the recessed position of the jaw allows the tongue to slip back toward the airway, leading to abnormal gaps in breathing, gasping, and choking and that the retruded lower jaw can restrict the airway, causing snoring or sleep apnea.  

In a January 2024 memorandum, a review of the Veteran's service records found that he did not participate in any toxic exposure risk activities.

In April 2024, an addendum opinion was obtained from the November 2023 examiner.  The examiner explained that the sleep apnea is less likely than not due to in-service respiratory infection.  The examiner explained that the Veteran's in-service respiratory infection was self-limiting and would not be present 60 years later.  The examiner also explained that his breathing was found to be unlabored and with no stridor during ear, nose, and throat physician treatment in April 2024.

After a careful review of the evidence of record, the Board finds that the evidence is persuasively against the claim of service connection for sleep apnea.  The Board determines the most probative evidence of record supports that the Veteran's sleep apnea did not have its onset during service and are not otherwise related to service, to include his in-service and post-service treatment.  The Board accords the most probative weight to the September 2018, November 2023, and April 2024 VA medical opinions.  In this regard, these examiner's findings and opinions are clear and unequivocal and are based on the relevant information, including the Veteran's statements, STRs, and post-service medical records.  In addition, the examiner's explanations are logical and follow from the facts and information given.  See Monzingo v. Shinseki, 26 Vet. App. 97, 105-06 (2012); Nieves-Rodriguez v. Peake, 22 Vet. App. 295, 304 (2008).

The September 2018 examiner explained that the Veteran's septal deviation is a condition distal to the anatomical structures involved in obstructive sleep apnea and is not a risk factor for the condition.  This examiner also explained that the sleep apnea is instead caused by a pathophysiologic episodic narrowing of the airway during sleep due to direct mechanical effects on the anatomy of the upper airway.  The November 2023 examiner explained that the Veteran has retrognathia that can physically cause disrupted breathing, snoring, and sleep apnea.  This examiner also explained that the Veteran's in-service respiratory infection was self-limiting and would not be present 60 years later.  The examiner supported this finding by explaining that his breathing was found to be unlabored and with no stridor during ear, nose, and throat physician treatment in April 2024.  The examiner considered the Veteran's lay statements, which was a concern of the JMR.

While the Veteran believes that he has sleep apnea is related to service, this is a complex medical question outside the competence of a non-medical expert to determine whether such a cause-and-effect relationship exists in this particular case.  Thus, this nexus question requires expert consideration and cannot be considered within the competence of a non-expert lay witness.  The Veteran, as a lay person, has not established the competence needed to rebut the expert medical opinion in this case.  See Fountain v. McDonald, 27 Vet. App. 258, 274-75 (2015); Monzingo, 26 Vet. App. at 106.  As such, the Veteran's opinion is not adequate to rebut the September 2018, November 2023, and April 2024 VA medical opinions, nor is it otherwise sufficiently probative to be considered competent evidence tending to increase the likelihood of a positive nexus between service and sleep apnea.

The Board notes that the Veteran has claimed during the period on appeal that he has experienced breathing problems ever since the in-service upper respiratory infections.  In rendering a decision on appeal, the Board must analyze the credibility and probative value of the evidence, account for the evidence which it finds to be persuasive or unpersuasive, and provide the reasons for its rejection of any material evidence favorable to the claimant.  Gilbert v. Derwinski, 1 Vet. App. 49, 57 (1990).  In this case, the Board finds Veteran's claims of experiencing breathing problems since service to be not credible.  The Veteran expressly denied a history of chronic or frequent colds, shortness of breath, pain or pressure in chest, and chronic cough in October 1962 and April 1967 reports of medical history.  In addition, a VA examiner explained in April 2024 that the Veteran's in-service respiratory infection was self-limiting and would not be present 60 years later and that his breathing was found to be unlabored and with no stridor during ear, nose, and throat physician treatment in April 2024.

(Continued on the next page)

?

The Board finds that the Veteran's own contemporaneous denial of relevant symptoms in October 1962 and April 1967 as well as the April 2024 VA examiner opinion are more probative than his claim made in the course of seeking VA compensation of experiencing ongoing breathing problems from an in-service respiratory infection for 60 years.  See Caluza v. Brown, 7 Vet. App. 498, 511 (1995) ("The credibility of a witness can be impeached by a showing of...inconsistent statements."), aff'd, 78 F.3d 604 (Fed. Cir. 1996).  In addition, in weighing credibility, VA may consider bias and self-interest in weighing the credibility of evidence.  Id.  As the Board finds the Veteran's claim of experiencing ongoing respiratory symptoms from an in-service respiratory infection for 60 years not credible, it is insufficient to establish that the Veteran's sleep apnea is related to service.

Accordingly, the evidence is persuasively against the claim.  As there is not an approximate balance of positive and negative evidence, the benefit-of-the-doubt doctrine is not applicable and service connection for sleep apnea is not warranted.  See 38 U.S.C. § 5107(b); 38 C.F.R. § 3.102.

 

 

RYAN T. KESSEL

Veterans Law Judge

Board of Veterans' Appeals

Attorney for the Board	Jimerfield, David

The Board's decision in this case is binding only with respect to the instant matter decided. This decision is not precedential and does not establish VA policies or interpretations of general applicability. 38 C.F.R. § 20.1303.

title: BVA Decision 25000002
text:
Citation Nr: 25000002
Decision Date: 01/02/25	Archive Date: 01/02/25

DOCKET NO. 17-27 479
DATE:    January 2, 2025

REMANDED

1. Entitlement to service connection for type 2 diabetes mellitus, to include as due to herbicide agent exposure, is remanded.

2. Entitlement to service connection for right lower extremity peripheral neuropathy, to include as due to herbicide agent exposure, is remanded.

3. Entitlement to service connection for left lower extremity peripheral neuropathy, to include as due to herbicide agent exposure, is remanded.

REASONS FOR REMAND

The Veteran served on active duty in the United States Army from July 31, 1973, to July 22, 1975.

In June 2021, the Veteran testified at a virtual hearing before the undersigned Veterans Law Judge. 

In a September 2021 decision, the Board denied entitlement to service connection for type 2 diabetes mellitus and peripheral neuropathy of the bilateral lower extremity. The Veteran appealed the September 2021 decision to the United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims (Court). In March 2023, the Court issued a Memorandum Decision finding that the Board had not adequately discussed the Veteran's credibility with regard to his assertion that he handled barrels containing chemicals that he believed to be herbicides and that the Board had not properly considered the articles submitted by the Veteran. The Court vacated the September 2021 Board decision and remanded the issues to the Board for further adjudication. 

In an August 2023 decision, the Board denied the claims for service connection for type 2 diabetes mellitus and for peripheral neuropathy of the bilateral lower extremity. The Veteran appealed the August 2023 decision to the Court. In August 2024, the Veteran and the Secretary of VA (parties) filed a Joint Motion for Remand (Joint Motion) to vacate the Board's decision and remand the claim. Specifically, the parties agreed that the Board must consider whether the Veteran is entitled to VA examinations for the disabilities on appeal due to experiencing certain symptoms during service. The Court granted the motion, and the case returned to the Board for further appellate review.

1. Entitlement to service connection for type 2 diabetes mellitus, to include as due to herbicide agent exposure, is remanded.

2. Entitlement to service connection for right lower extremity peripheral neuropathy, to include as due to herbicide agent exposure, is remanded.

3. Entitlement to service connection for left lower extremity peripheral neuropathy, to include as due to herbicide agent exposure, is remanded.

In an August 1973 service treatment record (STR), the Veteran was found to have diarrhea. In another August 1973 STR, the Veteran reported experiencing leg cramps. At the May 1975 Report of Medical Examination at separation from service, the Veteran reported a history of frequent headaches and of recent weight gain or loss. The parties agreed that the Board should consider whether these symptoms were indicative of diabetes and/or peripheral neuropathy during service, and whether such consideration warranted a VA examination. 

VA must provide a medical examination and/or medical opinion when there is (1) competent evidence of a current disability or persistent or recurrent symptoms of a disability, (2) evidence establishing that an event, injury, or disease occurred in service, or establishing certain diseases manifesting during an applicable presumptive period for which the claimant qualifies, and (3) an indication that the disability or persistent or recurrent symptoms of a disability may be associated with the veteran's service or with another service-connected disability, but (4) there is insufficient competent medical evidence on file for the Secretary to make a decision on the claim. McLendon v. Nicholson, 20 Vet. App. 79 (2006).

Here, as there is a medical question as to whether the Veteran's in-service symptoms are attributable to diabetes and peripheral neuropathy, and there is a current diagnosis for both conditions, the Board finds that these issues must be remanded to afford the Veteran a VA examination and opinion. 

The matters are REMANDED for the following action:

Schedule a VA examination and obtain an opinion from an appropriate clinician to determine the nature and etiology of diabetes mellitus type 2 and of peripheral neuropathy of the bilateral lower extremity. The examiner should have access to the Veteran's claims file. 

The agency of original jurisdiction must provide a copy of the below facts to the examiner. 

To assist in a review of the claims file, the examiner is informed of the following facts with citations in the record, when applicable: 

"	The Veteran served on active duty from July 31, 1973, to July 22, 1975.

"	The Veteran contends that type 2 diabetes mellitus and peripheral neuropathy of the bilateral lower extremity may have had their onset during service. 

"	An August 1973 service treatment record (STR) shows that the Veteran was seen with complaints of diarrhea for 3 days. He denied stomach cramps and reported having 3 bowel movements this morning. He described his stools as liquid brown in consistency. The examiner entered an impression of diarrhea. See VBMS entry with Document Type, "STR - Medical," Receipt Date 10/21/2013, at p. 4.

"	A Report of Medical Examination from May 1975 at separation from service shows that that the Veteran was found to have clinically normal evaluations of his endocrine system (item 22), lower extremities (item 37), and neurologic system (item 41). See VBMS entry with Document Type, "STR - Medical," Receipt Date 10/21/2013, at p. 23.

"	A May 1975 Report of Medical History shows that the Veteran denied a history of eye trouble, sugar or albumin in the urine, frequent or painful urination, lameness, neuritis, and paralysis. The Veteran reported a positive history of frequent headaches, recent weight gain or loss, and leg cramps, which he stated, "were related to service." (Item 11.) The examiner documented that the Veteran reported that he experienced headaches and fatigue after a head injury the previous year. The examiner documented the Veteran was treated in the emergency room and released. He had no loss of consciousness. He was dazed and confused at that time. (Item 25.) See VBMS entry with Document Type, "STR - Medical," Receipt Date 10/21/2013, at pp. 12-13.

"	The Veteran alleges that his in-service complaints of diarrhea, headaches, weight gain, and fatigue may have been indications of diabetes mellitus. Additionally, he believes that his positive report of leg cramps may be a symptom of peripheral neuropathy. 

"	A July 2010 private medical record shows that the Veteran was seen for abdominal pain. In addressing the Veteran's past medical history, the examiner documented that the Veteran had a history of diabetes "for at  least 12 years." See VBMS entry with Document Type, "Medical Treatment Record - Non-Government Facility," Receipt Date 05/01/2013, at p. 1.

"	This would indicate that the Veteran's diabetes mellitus was diagnosed at least by 1998.

"	A July 2015 VA treatment record shows that the Veteran was seen, and the examiner noted that the Veteran's blood sugars were not on goal. The Veteran's a1c was noted to be 11. In the Impression and Plan, the examiner wrote that the Veteran had DM2 with neuropathy, which the examiner documented was uncontrolled. The examiner documented the Veteran would be started on Gabapentin for the neuropathy. See VBMS entry with Document Type, "CAPRI," Receipt Date 04/06/2017, at pp. 312-313. 

"	The examiner's review of the record is NOT restricted to the evidence listed above. This list is provided to assist the examiner in locating potentially relevant evidence.

The examiner is asked to answer the following questions:

(a.) Are the Veteran's reports of diarrhea, headaches, weight gain or loss, and fatigue during service indicative of diabetes mellitus type 2? Please explain upon what facts, medical principles, and/or medical literature the opinion is based.

(b.) Did the Veteran's diabetes mellitus type 2 have its onset during the Veteran's service from July 1973 to July 1975 or is it otherwise related to service? Please explain upon what facts, medical principles, and/or medical literature the opinion is based.

(c.) Are the Veteran's reports of leg cramps during service indicative of peripheral neuropathy of the bilateral lower extremity? Please explain upon what facts, medical principles, and/or medical literature the opinion is based.

(d.) Did the Veteran's peripheral neuropathy of the bilateral lower extremity have its onset during his service from July 1973 to July 1975 or is otherwise related to service? Please explain upon what facts, medical principles, and/or medical literature the opinion is based.

If the examiner is unable to provide an opinion without resorting to mere speculation, he or she should explain why this is so. The examiner shall then explain whether the inability to provide a more definitive opinion is the result of a need for more information and indicate what additional evidence is necessary, or whether he or she has exhausted the limits of current medical knowledge in providing an answer to the question.

 

 

A. P. SIMPSON

Veterans Law Judge

Board of Veterans' Appeals

Attorney for the Board	Husain, Rahat

The Board's decision in this case is binding only with respect to the instant matter decided. This decision is not precedential and does not establish VA policies or interpretations of general applicability. 38 C.F.R. § 20.1303.

title: BVA Decision 25000003
text:
Citation Nr: 25000003
Decision Date: 01/02/25	Archive Date: 01/02/25

DOCKET NO. 16-01 951
DATE: January 2, 2025

ORDER

Entitlement to a separate 10 percent disability rating for service-connected left knee disability based on the presence of arthritis is granted, effective August 10, 2011, through March 22, 2018, subject to the laws and regulations governing the payment of monetary benefits.

Entitlement to a separate 10 percent disability rating for service-connected left knee disability based on instability is granted, effective August 10, 2011, through March 22, 2018, subject to the laws and regulations governing the payment of monetary benefits.

Entitlement to a rating in excess of 20 percent for service-connected left knee total post-prosthetic replacement of knee (left knee disability) based on dislocated semilunar cartilage prior to March 23, 2018, is denied.

Entitlement to a rating in excess of 60 percent for service-connected left knee disability from May 1, 2019, is denied.

Entitlement to an initial rating in excess of 20 percent for service-connected left ankle tendonitis (left ankle disability) is denied.

REMANDED

Entitlement to an initial rating in excess of 20 percent prior to June 14, 2023, and in excess of 30 percent thereafter, for service-connected right shoulder rotator cuff tear with subacromial/subdeltoid bursitis (right shoulder disability) is remanded.

Entitlement to a compensable rating prior to October 23, 2020, and in excess of 40 percent thereafter, for service-connected right upper extremity radiculopathy is remanded.

FINDINGS OF FACT

1. Prior to March 23, 2018, the Veteran's service-connected left knee disability was manifested by dislocated semilunar cartilage with frequent episodes of locking, pain, and effusion into the joint; mild instability; and arthritis with limited motion.  Nevertheless, it was not manifested by incapacitating exacerbations; moderate instability; flexion limited to 45 degrees; and/or extension limited to 10 degrees.

2. Since May 1, 2019, the Veteran has been in receipt of the maximum rating available under Diagnostic Code 5055, and a higher rating is precluded by the amputation rule.

3. At no time during the appeal period was the Veteran's left ankle disability manifested by ankylosis.

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

1. Resolving all reasonable doubt in the Veteran's favor, the criteria for a 10 percent disability rating for his service-connected left knee disability based X-ray evidence of arthritis in a major joint is granted, effective August 10, 2011, through March 22, 2018. 38 U.S.C. §§ 1155, 5107; 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.400 (o)(2), 4.1, 4.3, 4.7, 4.40, 4.45, 4.59, 4.71a, Diagnostic Code 5003.

2. Resolving all reasonable doubt in the Veteran's favor, the criteria for a 10 percent disability rating for service-connected left knee disability based on mild instability is granted, effective August 10, 2011, through March 22, 2018. 38 U.S.C. §§ 1155, 5107; 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.400 (o)(2), 4.1, 4.3, 4.7, 4.40, 4.45, 4.59, 4.71a, Diagnostic Code 5257.

3. The criteria for a rating in excess of 20 percent for service-connected left knee disability are not met. 38 U.S.C. §§ 1155, 5107; 38 C.F.R. §§ 4.1, 4.3, 4.7, 4.40, 4.45, 4.59, 4.71a, Diagnostic Codes 5258, 5260-5261.

4. The criteria for a rating in excess of 60 percent for service-connected left knee disability from May 1, 2019, are not met. 38 U.S.C. §§ 1155, 5107; 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.102, 3.159, 4.71a, Diagnostic Code 5055.

5. The criteria for an initial rating in excess of 20 percent for service-connected left ankle disability are not met. 38 U.S.C. §§ 1155, 5107; 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.102, 3.159, 4.71a, Diagnostic Code 5055.

REASONS AND BASES FOR FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS

The Veteran served on active duty in the United States Army from June 1977 to June 1980, with prior inactive service.  

These matters come to the Board of Veterans' Appeals (Board) from May 2012 and October 2015 rating decisions of the Department of Veteran Affairs (VA) Regional Office (RO) in San Juan, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico.  The Veteran expressed timely disagreement with the determinations relating to the issues listed on the title page, and the present appeal ensued.

These issues were previously before the Board in December 2021, at which time the issues were remanded for further development.

Increased Ratings

Disability evaluations are determined by the application of the facts presented to VA's Schedule for Rating Disabilities (Rating Schedule) at 38 C.F.R. Part 4. The percentage ratings contained in the Rating Schedule represent, as far as can be practicably determined, the average impairment in earning capacity resulting from diseases and injuries incurred or aggravated during military service and the residual conditions in civilian occupations. 38 U.S.C. § 1155; 38 C.F.R. § 4.1.

A veteran's entire history is to be considered when making disability evaluations. See generally 38 C.F.R. § 4.1; Schafrath v. Derwinski, 1 Vet. App. 589 (1995). Where an increase in the level of a service-connected disability is at issue, the primary concern is the present level of disability. Francisco v. Brown, 7 Vet. App. 55 (1994). However, where the question for consideration is entitlement to a higher initial rating assigned following the grant of service connection, evaluation of the medical evidence since the effective date of the grant of service connection and consideration of the appropriateness of "staged rating" (assignment of different ratings for distinct periods of time, based on the facts found) is required. Fenderson v. West, 12 Vet. App. 119, 126 (1999); see also Hart v. Mansfield, 21 Vet. App. 505 (2007).

Pyramiding that is, the evaluation of the same disability, or the same manifestation of a disability, under different diagnostic codes is to be avoided when evaluating a veteran's service-connected disability. 38 C.F.R. § 4.14. However, it is possible for a veteran to have separate and distinct manifestations from the same injury which would permit rating under several diagnostic codes; the critical element in permitting the assignment of several evaluations under various diagnostic codes is that none of the symptomatology for any one of the conditions is duplicative or overlapping with the symptomatology of the other condition. See Esteban v. Brown, 6 Vet. App. 259, 261-62 (1994).

Disability of the musculoskeletal system is primarily the inability, due to damage or infection in parts of the system, to perform the normal working movements of the body with normal excursion, strength, speed, coordination and endurance. Functional loss may be due to the absence or deformity of structures or other pathology, or it may be due to pain, supported by adequate pathology and evidenced by the visible behavior in undertaking the motion. Weakness is as important as limitation of motion, and a part that becomes painful on use must be regarded as seriously disabled. 38 C.F.R. § 4.40. In Mitchell v. Shinseki, 25 Vet. App. 32 (2011), the Court held that, although pain may cause a functional loss, "pain itself does not rise to the level of functional loss as contemplated by VA regulations applicable to the musculoskeletal system." Rather, pain may result in functional loss, but only if it limits the ability "to perform the normal working movements of the body with normal excursion, strength, speed, coordination, or endurance." Id., quoting 38 C.F.R. § 4.40.

With respect to joints, in particular, the factors of disability reside in reductions of normal excursion of movements in different planes. Inquiry will be directed to more or less than normal movement, weakened movement, excess fatigability, incoordination, pain on movement, swelling, deformity or atrophy of disuse. 38 C.F.R. § 4.45.

The intent of the Rating Schedule is to recognize actually painful, unstable or malaligned joints, due to healed injury, as entitled to at least the minimum compensable rating for the joint. 38 C.F.R. § 4.59. In Burton v. Shinseki, 25 Vet. App. 1, 5 (2011), the Court found that, when 38 C.F.R. § 4.59 is raised by the claimant or reasonably raised by the record, even in non-arthritis contexts, the Board should address its applicability.

1. Left Knee Disability

By way of background, a February 1985 rating decision assigned a 20 percent disability rating to the Veteran's service-connected left knee disability under Diagnostic Code 5258, effective August 1, 1984.

Thereafter, an August 2018 rating decision assigned a temporary total disability rating under Diagnostic Code 5055, effective March 23, 2018, following the Veteran's total knee replacement.  It then assigned a 30 percent rating under Diagnostic Code 5055, effective May 1, 2019.

Thereafter, in a May 2021 rating decision, the agency of original jurisdiction (AOJ) awarded an increased rating of 60 percent under Diagnostic Code 5055, effective May 1, 2019.

Under Diagnostic Code 5003, which deals with degenerative arthritis, when range of motion is not limited or limited only to a noncompensable degree, a minimum rating of 10 percent is assigned for each major joint or group of minor joints affected by limitation of motion, to be combined, not added. 38 C.F.R. § 4.71a, Diagnostic Code 5003. Limited motion must be confirmed by swelling, muscle spasm or satisfactory evidence of painful motion. When limited motion, but X-ray evidence of involvement of 2 or more major joints or 2 or more minor joint groups, a 10 percent disability rating is warranted; if there is evidence of occasional incapacitation exacerbations, a 20 percent disability rating is warranted. Id.

The Board notes that, during the pendency of the appeal, VA revised the rating criteria for Diagnostic Codes 5055 and 5257, effective February 7, 2021. See 85 Fed. Reg. 76453 (November 30, 2020). When the regulations concerning entitlement to a higher rating are changed during the course of an appeal, the veteran may be entitled to resolution of his claim under the criteria that are to his advantage. The former rating criteria may be applied throughout the period of the appeal if they are more favorable to him. The revised rating criteria may be applied only prospectively, however, from the effective date of the change forward unless the regulatory change specifically permits retroactive application. 38 U.S.C. § 5110(g); VAOPGCPREC 7-03; VAOPGCPREC 3-00; Kuzma v. Principi, 341 F.3d 1327 (Fed. Cir. 2003).

Under the former rating criteria for Diagnostic Code 5055 (prior to the regulatory change on February 7, 2021), a 100 percent rating is provided for one year following implantation of prosthesis. After one year, a minimum 30 percent rating is provided. A maximum 60 percent is warranted for chronic residuals consisting of severe painful motion or weakness in the affected extremity. In addition, intermediate degrees of residual weakness, pain, or limitation of motion may be rated by analogy to Diagnostic Codes 5256, 5261, or 5262.

Under the current rating criteria for Diagnostic Code 5055 (as of February 7, 2021), a 100 percent rating is provided for four months following implantation of prosthesis. After four months, a minimum 30 percent evaluation, for "total replacements only" is provided. A maximum 60 percent is warranted for chronic residuals consisting of severe painful motion or weakness in the affected extremity. In addition, intermediate degrees of residual weakness, pain, or limitation of motion may be rated by analogy to Diagnostic Codes 5256, 5261, or 5262. Note: At the conclusion of the 100 percent evaluation period, evaluate resurfacing under diagnostic codes 5256 through 5262; there is no minimum evaluation for resurfacing.

Under the former rating criteria for Diagnostic Code 5257, a 10 percent disability rating is warranted for slight recurrent subluxation or lateral instability of the knee; a 20 percent rating is warranted for moderate recurrent subluxation or lateral instability of the knee; and a 30 percent rating is warranted for severe recurrent subluxation or lateral instability of the knee. 38 C.F.R. § 4.71a.

The Board observes that the words "mild," "moderate," and "severe" are not defined in the Rating Schedule. Rather than applying a mechanical formula, the Board must evaluate all of the evidence to the degree that its decisions are "equitable and just." See 38 C.F.R. § 4.6. It should also be noted that use of descriptive terminology such as "mild" by medical examiners, although an element of evidence to be considered by the Board, is not dispositive of an issue. All evidence must be evaluated in arriving at a decision regarding an increased rating. 38 U.S.C. § 7104(a); 38 C.F.R. §§ 4.2, 4.6.

Under Diagnostic Code 5258, a 20 percent disability rating is warranted for dislocated semilunar cartilage with frequent episodes of "locking," pain, and effusion. 38 C.F.R. § 4.71a.

Under Diagnostic Code 5260, a 10 percent disability rating is warranted for flexion of the knee limited to 45 degrees; a 20 percent rating is warranted for flexion of the knee limited to 30 degrees; and a 30 percent rating is warranted for flexion of the knee limited to 15 degrees. Id.

Under Diagnostic Code 5261, a 10 percent rating is warranted for extension of the knee limited to 10 degrees; a 20 percent rating is warranted for extension of the knee limited to 15 degrees; a 30 percent rating is warranted for extension of the knee limited to 20 degrees; a 40 percent for extension of the knee limited to 30 degrees, and 50 percent for extension of the knee limited to 45 degrees. Id.

The rating of the same disability under various diagnoses is to be avoided. 38 C.F.R. § 4.14. That does not preclude the assignment of separate ratings for separate and distinct symptomatology where none of the symptomatology justifying a rating under one diagnostic code is duplicative of or overlapping with the symptomatology justifying a rating under another diagnostic code. Esteban v. Brown, 6 Vet. App. 259 (1994). Further, the Court has held that the evaluation of a knee disability under Diagnostic Code 5257 and Diagnostic Codes 5260 or 5261 does not preclude, as a matter of law, a separate evaluation under Diagnostic Code 5258. See Lyles v. Shulkin, 29 Vet. App. 107 (2017).

In this regard, the Court has held that the rule against pyramiding does not categorically prohibit VA's assignment of separate evaluations under Diagnostic Code 5258 and Diagnostic Code 5257 if the veteran is assigned an evaluation under Diagnostic Code 5258 for meniscus symptoms that do not include lateral instability. See Walleman v. McDonough, 35 Vet. App. 294, 303-07 (2022). Indeed, following Walleman, the Court held, "Taken together, and Walleman direct VA, when considering the appropriate evaluation under a meniscal Diagnostic Code, to catalog a veteran's manifestations of a service-connected knee disability and the resulting functional impairment and assign all independently supportable knee evaluations that correspond with these manifestations." See Estevez v. McDonough, 36 Vet. App. 157, 169-170 (2023).

A.  Prior to March 23, 2018

Pertinent evidence of record includes the Veteran's treatment records and VA examination reports.

An August 2011 VA treatment record noted that the Veteran needed a total knee replacement, but he was not willing to undergo one at that time.  Also noted during the examination was a scar on the midline as a result of a meniscectomy.

In March 2012, the Veteran underwent a VA knee examination, and he was diagnosed with a left knee meniscus tear, status post meniscectomy.  He reported pain, aching, and swelling in his left knee, as well as frequent crepitus.  He also reported locking and giving way during ambulation.  He also reported flare-ups precipitated by walking and standing leading to pain.  Upon examination, he displayed flexion to 90 degrees, with objective evidence of pain at 55 degrees; and extension to zero degrees with no objective evidence of pain.  Following repetitive-use testing, his range of motion was the same.  The examiner indicated that the Veteran's functional loss included less movement than normal, pain on movement, and swelling.  There was also tenderness or pain to palpation.  Muscle strength and joint stability testing was normal.  As for the Veteran's history of a partial meniscectomy, the examiner noted that he experienced frequent episodes of locking, pain, and effusion.  The Veteran was noted to use a crutch on a constant basis, and the examiner noted that the Veteran had traumatic arthritis in his left knee based on X-rays.  As for the functional impairment associated with the Veteran's disability, the examiner noted that the Veteran needed to work at a sedentary position, must be allowed five-minute breaks every half hour, and that he could not perform light lifting.

An October 2014 VA treatment record noted that the Veteran had been involved in multiple falls secondary to left knee instability.

In September 2015, the Veteran underwent another VA knee examination.  He reported severe pain with a constant locking sensation and giving-way sensation.  He also reported flare-ups of the left knee, as well as difficulty climbing stairs and walking for a prolonged period.  Upon examination, he displayed flexion to 90 degrees, and extension to zero degrees, with evidence of pain with flexion, extension, and weight bearing; and there was evidence of crepitus.  There was also tenderness or pain to palpation.  Muscle strength testing was normal, and there was no evidence of ankylosis.  Joint stability testing was also normal, and there was no history of recurrent subluxation or lateral instability.

A November 2017 VA treatment record noted that no varus or valgus instability was present.

A March 2018 VA treatment record noted that the Veteran had sustained falls at his home due to knee instability.

Based on the evidence of record, the Board finds that the Veteran is entitled to a 10 percent disability rating under Diagnostic 5003 for X-ray evidence of arthritis in a major joint causing noncompensable limitation of motion, effective August 10, 2011, the day his claim for an increased rating was received.  As noted above, the March 2012 VA examiner noted that the Veteran experienced less movement than normal, and that traumatic arthritis had been found in his left knee based on X-rays.

Moreover, after resolving all reasonable doubt in the Veteran's favor, the Board finds that a separate 10 percent disability rating is warranted under Diagnostic Code 5257 for left knee instability, effective August 10, 2011, the day his claim for an increased rating was received.  As noted above, the March 2012 VA examination report noted the Veteran's report that his left knee would give way during ambulation, and the October 2014 VA treatment record noted that the Veteran had been involved in multiple falls secondary to left knee instability.  As such, the Board will resolve reasonable doubt in his favor and award a separate 10 percent disability rating under Diagnostic Code 5257 for mild instability in the left knee.

However, the Board finds that higher ratings are not warranted at any point prior to March 23, 2018.

As for Diagnostic Code 5003, there is no evidence indicating that the Veteran's left knee arthritis was manifested by occasional incapacitating exacerbations.  Although "incapacitating exacerbations" is not defined under Diagnostic Code 5003, the Board analogizes it to "incapacitating episodes," which is defined in the IVDS Formula at Note (1) as "a period of acute signs and symptoms... that requires bed rest prescribed by a physician and treatment by a physician." 38 C.F.R. § 4.71a, Diagnostic Code 5003, IVDS Formula at Note (1).  There is no indication that the Veteran's was prescribed bed rest by a physician as a result of the impairment associated with his service-connected left knee disability.  As such, a higher rating is not warranted under Diagnostic Code 5003.

While the Board notes that a higher rating could be assigned to the Veteran's service-connected left knee disability under Diagnostic Code 5256 for ankylosis of the knee, there is no evidence of record demonstrating ankylosis. Indeed, there is no indication of ankylosis throughout the appeal period. To the contrary, the Veteran displayed range of motion during the March 2012 VA examination, and the September 2015 VA examiner specifically indicated that ankylosis was not present in his left knee. Moreover, the evidence of record, including the VA examination reports, consistently reflect that he retained some range of motion in his left knee, even in consideration of functional loss due to repetitive use or during flare-ups.

As for Diagnostic Code 5260 concerning limitation of flexion, the Board notes that the Veteran's range of motion has never met the criteria for compensable ratings under that diagnostic code, let alone the criteria warranted for higher ratings. Indeed, the Veteran's flexion has consistently been found to be greater than 45 degrees (the criteria for a 10 percent rating under Diagnostic Code 5260). Instead, the Veteran has been assigned a 10 percent rating under Diagnostic Code 5003 for limited, albeit noncompensable, range of motion.

As for Diagnostic Code 5261 concerning limitation of extension, the Board notes that the Veteran's range of motion has never met the criteria for a compensable under that code. To the contrary, even when considering the functional impairment following repetitive use or during flare-ups, the Veteran's extension has consistently been found to be 5 degrees or greater. As noted above, to meet the criteria for a 10 percent rating under Diagnostic Code 5261, extension must be limited to 10 degrees.

With regard to giving proper consideration to the effects of pain in assigning a disability rating, as well as the provisions of 38 C.F.R. § 4.45 and the holdings in DeLuca and Mitchell, VA examination reports of record clearly reflect consideration of these principles. For example, the March 2012 VA examiner noted that the Veteran was able to perform repetitive-use testing, and the examiner noted that he did not have any additional limitation in range of motion or functional loss following repetitive use.  Thus, the evidence does not show that the Veteran's functional loss following repetitive use or during a flare-up would be of such frequency or severity to warrant higher ratings at any point during the appeal period.

With regard to Diagnostic Code 5258, the Veteran is currently assigned the maximum 20 percent disability rating available under the diagnostic code.  Moreover, insofar as a part of his meniscus was removed during the partial meniscectomy, any symptoms attributable to that surgery, such as locking, pain, and effusion, are compensated under Diagnostic Code 5258.  Thus, a separate rating under Diagnostic Code 5259 would constitute pyramiding.

Finally, as for Diagnostic Code 5257, the Board has also considered whether ratings in excess of those currently assigned are warranted at any point during the appeal period prior to March 23, 2018.  Although the evidence reflects the Veteran's report of instability, the March 2012 and September 2015 VA examination reports note that joint testing was normal.  Likewise, the November 2017 VA treatment record noted that no varus or valgus instability was present.  Thus, a rating higher than that currently assigned (10 percent) for the period prior to March 23, 2018, is not warranted, as only mild instability, at best, is shown by the record.

B.  From May 1, 2019

With regard to the period from May 1, 2019, as noted above, the August 2018 rating decision assigned a temporary total disability rating under Diagnostic Code 5055, effective March 23, 2018, following the Veteran's total knee replacement.  It then assigned a 30 percent rating under Diagnostic Code 5055, effective May 1, 2019.

Thereafter, in a May 2021 rating decision, the AOJ awarded an increased rating of 60 percent under Diagnostic Code 5055, effective May 1, 2019.

A 60 percent rating is the maximum disability rating available under Diagnostic Code 5055 and is assigned for chronic residuals consisting of severe painful motion or weakness in the affected extremity. The assignment of separate ratings for manifestations of the knee not contemplated by Diagnostic Code 5055 are precluded by the amputation rule. 

The amputation rule provides that the combined rating for disabilities of an extremity shall not exceed the rating for the amputation of the extremity. 38 C.F.R. § 4.6. An amputation of the knee is rated at 60 percent under Diagnostic Code 5162 for an amputation of the leg at a place two thirds of the way between the knee joint and perineum. 

Because the Veteran is currently rated at the maximum rating available under Diagnostic Code 5055; and because a rating higher than 60 percent is precluded by the amputation rule, the Veteran's request for a higher rating is denied.

In summation, the Board finds that a 10 percent disability rating is warranted under Diagnostic Code 5003 for left knee arthritis, effective August 10, 2011, through March 22, 2018.  Moreover, a 10 percent disability rating is warranted under Diagnostic Code 5257 for mild instability associated with the service-connected left knee disability, effective August 10, 2011, through March 22, 2018. However, the weight of the probative evidence is against higher ratings at any other point during the appeal period.

C.  Left Ankle Disability

By way of background, the October 2015 rating decision on appeal awarded service connection for the Veteran's left ankle disability, and it assigned an initial 20 percent disability rating under Diagnostic Code 5271, effective March 2, 2015.

Under diagnostic code 5271, a 20 percent rating is warranted for marked limited motion of the ankle. 38 C.F.R. § 4.71a, Diagnostic Code 5271. This is the maximum rating available under diagnostic code 5271. As such, the Board will consider whether a higher rating is available under another diagnostic code, 5270, pertaining to disability manifested by ankylosis of the ankle.

Under Diagnostic code 5270, a minimum 20 percent rating is assigned for ankylosis of the ankle in plantar flexion, less than 30 degrees. A 30 percent rating is warranted for ankylosis of the ankle where plantar flexion is fixed between 30 and 40 degrees, or dorsiflexion is fixed between 0 and 10 degrees. A maximum 40 percent rating is warranted where plantar flexion is fixed at more than 40 degrees, or where dorsiflexion is fixed at more than 10 degrees with abduction, inversion, or eversion deformity. 38 C.F.R. § 4.71a, Diagnostic Code 5270. "Ankylosis" is defined as "immobility and consolidation of a joint due to disease, injury, or surgical procedure." See Lewis v. Derwinski, 3 Vet. App. 259 (1992).

Other potentially applicable diagnostic codes include 5272 (ankylosis of the subastralgar or tarsal joint), 5273 (malunion of the os calcis or astralgus), and 5274 (astralgalectomy). 38 C.F.R. § 4.71a, Diagnostic Codes 5272, 5273, and 5274. As the Veteran has not been shown to have these disabilities at any time during the appeal period, however, these diagnostic codes are not applicable herein.

In July 2015, the Veteran underwent a VA examination, and he was diagnosed with left ankle tendonitis.  He reported a constant pain, ranging from seven to ten, that increased with physical activities, standing, or walking.  He denied flare-ups, but he reported problems with walking and climbing stairs.  Upon examination, the examiner noted that there was no evidence of ankylosis.

In April 2021, the Veteran underwent another examination, and he reported constant pain and swelling in his left ankle that worsened with walking.  He also reported flare-ups, when he would be unable to walk or stand.  The examiner noted that the Veteran did not have ankylosis.  Moreover, insofar as the Veteran reported flare-ups, the examiner noted that he would still retain some range of motion in the joint.

In October 2023, the Veteran underwent another examination, and he reported a limited ability to run, walk for prolonged periods, bend, squat, or bear weight. He also denied flare-ups. The examiner noted that the Veteran did not have ankylosis.  Moreover, with regard to repeated use, the examiner noted that his left ankle range of motion would not be further limited.

As noted above, a 20 percent rating is the highest rating afforded under the rating schedule for limitation of motion of the ankle. The Board has considered whether an additional evaluation might be warranted under another diagnostic code for the ankle, but finds that this is not the case. Specifically, to warrant evaluation under Diagnostic Code 5270, there must be evidence of ankylosis. To warrant evaluation under Diagnostic Code 5272, there must be ankylosis of the subastragalar or tarsal joint. To warrant evaluation under Diagnostic Code 5273, there must be malunion of the os calcis or astragalus. To warrant evaluation under Diagnostic Code 5274, there must be astragalectomy. 

Quite simply, there is no evidence of record to demonstrate that any of these diagnostic codes are relevant to the Veteran's symptoms.  Indeed, each of the VA examiners of record have indicated that the Veteran did not suffer from ankylosis.

In summation, as the weight of the probative evidence is against a higher rating at any point during the appeal period, the Veteran's claim must be denied.

REASONS FOR REMAND

As noted in the prior Board remand, in a May 2021 rating decision, the AOJ combined the initial evaluation assigned for the Veteran's service-connected right shoulder disability, with the initial evaluation assigned to the Veteran's service-connected radiculopathy of the right arm for rating purposes, effective October 23, 2020.

Thereafter, in December 2023, the AOJ separated the two disabilities.  It then assigned an initial 40 percent disability rating to the Veteran's right upper extremity radiculopathy, effective October 23, 2020.  As for the Veteran's right shoulder disability, it awarded an increased rating of 40 percent, effective June 14, 2023.

In the December 2021 remand, the Board determined that the evidence of record was insufficient to adjudicate the Veteran's claims for increased ratings for his service-connected right shoulder disability and right upper extremity radiculopathy because the most recent examination of record did not sufficiently distinguish between the symptoms associated with each disability to address the appealed issues.  Thus, the Board directed the AOJ to schedule the Veteran for VA examinations that addressed the severity, frequency, and duration of all symptoms attributable to the Veteran's service-connected right shoulder disability and radiculopathy of the right arm.  If any muscle was damaged, the examiner was directed to identify the damaged muscle and the muscle group; and to describe the level of functional impairment associated with the muscle injury/injuries.

 A VA shoulder examination was conducted in June 2023; however, the examiner did not attempt to distinguish between the symptoms attributable to service-connected right shoulder disability from the symptoms attributable to his radiculopathy of the right arm.  

The Veteran was then afforded a VA peripheral nerves examination in September 2023.  Although the examiner acknowledged the Veteran's right shoulder disability, in addition to his right upper extremity radiculopathy, the examiner did not distinguish between the functional impairment attributable to each disability.  Instead, the examiner stated that, while he believed that the Veteran had an incomplete tear of the right rotator cuff, there was no MRI of record to confirm.

In September 2023, an addendum opinion was obtained in an attempt to address the full nature and severity of the Veteran's service-connected disabilities; however, the Board notes that the opinion was by a different VA examiner, and it did not involve an actual examination of the Veteran.

In October 2023, the Veteran underwent a VA muscle examination; however, the examiner noted that the most recent imaging of the Veteran's right shoulder was performed in April 2013.

In December 2023, the AOJ requested a new VA examination citing the September 2023 VA examination's notation that the Veteran may have an incomplete tear of the right rotator cuff, but that there was no MRI of record to confirm.  The AOJ directed the examiner that, if further testing was needed, please perform such testing.  Unfortunately, however, it does not appear that further testing was performed.  Instead, the examiner noted the April 2013 MRI once again and stated that it was unclear if there was a current tear since there was no evidence based on recent imagining to ascertain the condition of the underlying tear.

Because the recent VA examinations indicate that imaging is necessary to determine the current nature and severity of the Veteran's right shoulder disability, and to distinguish between the function impairment associated with his right shoulder disability and his right upper extremity radiculopathy, new examinations are necessary.

On remand, the AOJ should obtain any outstanding VA treatment records that are not currently associated with the claims file. Additionally, the Veteran should be given the opportunity to identify any outstanding pertinent evidence.

The matters are REMANDED for the following action:

1. Associate with the claims file any outstanding VA treatment records.

2. Give the Veteran an additional opportunity to submit or identify any outstanding evidence pertinent to his claims remaining on appeal. The AOJ should then attempt to obtain those records if he provides the appropriate authorization.

3. The Veteran should be scheduled for appropriate VA examinations to determine the current nature and severity of his service-connected right shoulder disability and right upper extremity radiculopathy. The entire record must be made available to, and be reviewed by, the examiner, and the examination report should note that review. Any indicated evaluations, studies, and tests, to include an MRI of the right shoulder, must be conducted as prior examiners have indicated that the April 2013 MRI is stale. The examiner should take a history from the Veteran as to the progression of his service-connected right shoulder disability and right upper extremity radiculopathy.

a) The examiner should describe all symptoms associated with the Veteran's service-connected right shoulder disability and right upper extremity radiculopathy. 

With regard to the Veteran's right shoulder disability, the examiner is asked to discuss the anatomy of the Veteran's right shoulder in terms congruent with the applicable rating criteria (former and current) pertinent to all parts of the shoulder, to include the Muscle Groups involved.  If any muscle(s) affecting the right rotator cuff are damaged, the examiner must identify the damaged muscle, the Muscle Group, and describe the level of functional impairment associated with the muscle injury/injuries.

b) The examiner should conduct range of motion testing (expressed in degrees) in active motion, passive motion, weight-bearing, and nonweight-bearing. If pain is noted on range-of-motion testing, the examiner must specify at what point his loss of range of motion was due to pain and at what point the evidence of pain ended.

c)  The examiner should ask the Veteran to report any range of motion loss during flare-ups or following repeated use. He should be asked to identify: (1) the frequency of flare-ups; (2) the duration of flare-ups; (3) any precipitating factors; and (4) any alleviating factors. Even if the Veteran is not experiencing a flare-up at the time of the examination, the examiner must elicit relevant information as to flare ups and ask him to describe the additional functional loss, to include loss of range of motion, if any, he suffers during flare-ups or following repeated use. 

If the examination does not occur during a flare-up or following repetitive use, based upon the evidence of record, and the information elicited on examination, the examiner should estimate range of motion loss during a flare-up and/or after repetitive use, if any. If an estimate cannot be provided based on the information provided by the Veteran and the contemporaneous medical evidence available, the examiner should state so clearly and provide a detailed explanation as to whether such estimates would be unknowable to the medical community to any degree of medical certainty, in spite of such evidence.

d)  With regard to the Veteran's right upper extremity radiculopathy, the examiner should indicate whether there is complete or incomplete paralysis of the affected nerve(s) and, if so, the examiner should describe the severity of the impairment as mild, moderate, or severe with marked muscular atrophy.

In addressing such inquiries, the examiner should take into consideration all of the evidence of record, to include medical records as well as the Veteran's lay statements, accepted medical principles and objective medical findings.

All examination findings/testing results, along with a complete, clearly stated rationale for any opinion offered, must be provided.

4. Thereafter, readjudicate the appeal.

 

 

Leetra J. Harris

Veterans Law Judge

Board of Veterans' Appeals

Attorney for the Board	James R. Springer, Counsel
