title: BVA Decision 25000004: Entitlement to an earlier effective date of November 10, 2003, for the claim of service connection for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is granted
text:
Citation Nr: 25000004
Decision Date: 01/02/25	Archive Date: 01/02/25

DOCKET NO. 17-16 766
DATE: January 2, 2025

ORDER

Entitlement to an earlier effective date of November 10, 2003, for the claim of service connection for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is granted.

FINDING OF FACT

On November 10, 2003 the Veteran submitted a claim for service connection for PTSD that was not finally adjudicated until January 5, 2015, which the Veteran timely appealed.

CONCLUSION OF LAW

The criteria for an earlier effective date of November 10, 2003, for the grant of service connection for PTSD, have been met. 38 U.S.C. § 5100; 38 C.F.R. § 3.400.

REASONS AND BASES FOR FINDING AND CONCLUSION

The Veteran served honorably on active duty in the United States Navy from May 1988 to July 1989.

This matter is before the Board of Veterans' Appeals (Board) on appeal from an April 2016 rating decision issued by the Department of Veterans Affairs agency of original jurisdiction (AOJ). 

In April 2020, the Veteran testified at a Travel Board hearing before a Veterans Law Judge who is no longer at the Board. The AOJ notified the Veteran of the opportunity for another hearing, for which no response was received. A transcript of the hearing is associated with the claims file.

The Veteran appealed the Board's July 30, 2020 decision to the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims (CAVC). In May 2024, CAVC issued a memorandum decision. In relevant part, the CAVC decision found remand of the Veteran's claim was warranted because the Board failed to provide an adequate statement of reasons and bases regarding whether the Veteran was properly notified of his right to appeal the July 27, 2004 VA administrative decision and whether a July 24, 2006 VA treatment report should have been construed as an informal claim for benefits under the regulations in effect at the time.

This appeal has been advanced on the Board's docket pursuant to 38 C.F.R. § 20.902(c).

Entitlement to an earlier effective date, of November 10, 2003, for the claim of service connection for PTSD.

The Veteran seeks an earlier effective date for the grant of service connection for PTSD. See November 2016 Notice of Disagreement. He seeks the date of November 10, 2003, which is the date he filed his initial claim for PTSD.

The effective date of an award of compensation shall be fixed in accordance with the facts found but shall not be earlier than the date of receipt of application therefor. 38 U.S.C. § 5110(a). The effective date of an award of compensation based on a claim reopened after a final disallowance will be the date of receipt of the claim to reopen, or the date entitlement arose, whichever is later. 38 C.F.R. § 3.400(q)(2), (r).

Regulations governing what constitutes a claim were revised effective March 24, 2015. As the Veteran's claim was received prior to that date, the Board must apply the older regulations. Prior to March 24, 2015, a claim was "a formal or informal communication in writing requesting a determination of entitlement, or evidencing a belief in entitlement, to a benefit." 38 C.F.R. § 3.1(p). An informal claim was "[a]ny communication or action indicating intent to apply for one or more benefits." 38 C.F.R. § 3.155(a).

The currently assigned effective date of December 21, 2009 is based on the date the Veteran filed a VA Form 21-526EZ claim for service connection for PTSD. See January 2015 rating decision. The AOJ had previously denied the Veteran's November 2003 claim in a July 27, 2004 letter notifying the Veteran that a July 14, 2004 administrative decision documented the Veteran's character of discharge was a bar to receiving VA benefits. See July 27, 2004 AOJ correspondence. 

Although the AOJ next provided a statement of the case on the issue of whether the Veteran's character of discharge constituted a bar to VA benefits in May 2011, and a supplemental statement of the case on that matter in July 2012, the AOJ did not address the claim for service connection for PTSD until 2015. On January 5, 2015, the AOJ issued a rating decision on the PTSD claim granting service connection for PTSD at a 100 percent disability rating, in response to a Board decision finding the Veteran's character of discharge was not a bar to VA benefits. See January 2014 Board decision. 

In general, if a veteran does not appeal a VA decision, that decision becomes final. See Cook v. Principi, 318 F.3d 1334, 1336 (Fed. Cir. 2002) (en banc). However, the VA must notify a veteran of his or her right to appeal the decision. 38 C.F.R. § 3.103(b)(1) (2004). Further, the VA must notify the veteran of the procedure to appeal, and the time limits within which he or she must appeal. Id. ("Such notice shall clearly set forth the decision made, any applicable effective date, the reason(s) for the decision, the right to a hearing on any issue involved in the claim, the right of representation and the right, as well as the necessary procedures and time limits, to initiate an appeal of the decision.").

If the VA fails to notify the veteran of this right, the claim remains open. 38 USCS §§ 7252(a), 7266 (2004); see also, Best v. Brown, 10 Vet. App. 322, 325 (1997) (finding that VA's failure to comply with notice requirements prevented a rating decision from becoming final). 

Here, the July 27, 2004 AOJ correspondence notified the Veteran of a decision that found he was not eligible for any VA benefits for his military service. It also notified the Veteran of the evidence the AOJ specifically considered. Further, it notified him that he may ask for a change in the character of his discharge, and/or apply for a correction, providing forms to do so. 

However, the July 27, 2004 AOJ correspondence did not notify the Veteran of his right to appeal the decision denying service connection for PTSD. It did not notify him of the time limits to appeal. Thus, the decision to deny service connection for PTSD did not become final. See, e.g., AG v. Peake, 536 F.3d 1306, 1308 (Fed. Cir. 2008) (finding the proceedings ongoing because of the VA's failure to notify the Veteran of his right to appeal). 

As the decision to deny the claim did not become final, the Veteran's claim remained open until the AOJ provided the proper notification on the PTSD claim. Here, the AOJ did not provide proper notice until issuing the January 2015 rating decision. See, e.g., AG v. Peake, 536 F.3d at 1310. 

Because the effective date of the award of service connection is based on the date that the application upon which service connection was eventually awarded was filed with the VA, the November 10, 2003 date is warranted. See, e.g., Lalonde v. West, 12 Vet. App. 377, 382 (1999); Juarez v. Peake, 21 Vet. App. 537, 544 (2008) (finding the subsequent rating decision, which properly provided notice and an opportunity to appeal was the proper effective date.). Thus, an earlier effective date, of November 10, 2003, for service connection for PTSD is granted.

There is no basis to grant an effective date earlier than November 10, 2003. This is because November 10, 2003 was the first date on which the VA received correspondence regarding the Veteran's PTSD claim for service connection. There are no documents dated prior to this on the matter. 38 U.S.C. § 5110(a); 38 C.F.R. § 3.400(q), (r).

Finally, having found the Veteran was not properly notified of his right to appeal the July 27, 2004 VA administrative decision, the Board finds it need not address the question of whether the July 24, 2006 VA treatment report should have been construed as an informal claim for benefits under the regulations in effect at the time.

 

 

Leetra J. Harris

Veterans Law Judge

Board of Veterans' Appeals

Attorney for the Board	Black, Julie A.

The Board's decision in this case is binding only with respect to the instant matter decided. This decision is not precedential and does not establish VA policies or interpretations of general applicability. 38 C.F.R. § 20.1303.

title: BVA Decision 25000005: Special monthly compensation based on the need for aid and attendance is granted, subject to the rules and regulations governing the payment of VA monetary benefits
text:
Citation Nr: 25000005
Decision Date: 01/02/25	Archive Date: 01/02/25

DOCKET NO. 16-49 436
DATE: January 2, 2025

ORDER

Special monthly compensation based on the need for aid and attendance is granted, subject to the rules and regulations governing the payment of VA monetary benefits.

FINDING OF FACT

The Veteran is shown to be in need of regular aid and attendance by reason of service-connected disability.  

CONCLUSION OF LAW

The criteria for special monthly compensation based on the need for regular aid and attendance of another person are met.  38 U.S.C. §§ 1114, 1502, 5107; 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.102, 3.350, 3.352.  

REASONS AND BASES FOR FINDING AND CONCLUSION

The Veteran had active-duty service from February 1967 to February 1971, to include service in the Republic of Vietnam.  

In July 2016, the RO denied a claim for SMC based on the need for aid and attendance.  

In March 2019, the Veteran was afforded a hearing before the undersigned.  

In April 2020, the Board denied the claim.  The Veteran appealed the decision to the United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims (Court).  In January 2021, the Court granted a Joint Motion for Remand (JMR).  In October 2022, the Board denied the claim a second time.  In July 2023, the Court granted a JMR.

The Board remanded the claim in March 2022 and January 2024.

In December 2024, a waiver of AOJ review was received.  Accordingly, a remand for AOJ review is not required.  38 C.F.R. § 20.1304 (c).  

1.  Special monthly compensation (SMC).

In November 2010, the RO granted special monthly pension based on the need for aid and attendance.  

In May 2011, the RO determined that the Veteran is not competent to handle disbursement of VA funds.  

In February 2016, the Veteran filed a claim for SMC.  See Veteran's VA Form 21-526EZ and VA Form 21-2680, received in February 2016.  In July 2016, the RO denied the claim.  The Veteran has appealed.  

Service connection is currently in effect for PTSD to include anxiety and depression, evaluated as 100 percent disabling effective June 8, 2010.     

The anatomical loss or loss of use of both feet, one hand and one foot, or loss of vision in both eyes, or is permanently bedridden or with such significant disabilities as to be in need or require the regular aid and attendance of another person under the criteria set forth in 38 C.F.R. § 3.352(a).  38 U.S.C. § 1114(l); 38 C.F.R. § 3.350 (b)(3).  

When determining whether the regular aid and attendance of another person is needed, the following factors are considered: inability to dress or undress oneself, or to keep oneself ordinarily clean and presentable; frequent need of adjustment of any special prosthetic or orthopedic appliances which by reason of the particular disability cannot be done without such aid; inability to feed oneself through the loss of coordination of upper extremities or through extreme weakness; inability to attend to the wants of nature; or an incapacity, physical or mental, which requires care or assistance on a regular basis to protect the Veteran from the hazards or dangers incident to his or her daily environment.  38 C.F.R. § 3.352 (a).

For the purposes of 38 C.F.R. § 3.352 (a), "bedridden" is a proper basis for determining whether the veteran needs regular aid and attendance of another person.  "Bedridden" means that the veteran is actually required to remain in bed.  38 C.F.R. §§ 3.350 (b)(4), 3.352(a).  Voluntarily taking to bed or being prescribed bed rest for the greater or lesser part of the day to promote convalescence or cure is insufficient.  Determinations that the veteran is so helpless as to be in need of regular aid and attendance will not be based solely upon an opinion that the veteran's condition is such as would require them to be in bed but must be based on the actual requirement of personal assistance from others.  38 C.F.R. § 3.352 (a).

A veteran does not need to demonstrate all the above factors to be found entitled to aid and attendance benefits, and the need for regular aid and attendance does not have to be constant.  The Veteran does not have the loss or loss of use of the feet or hands or vision deficits.  The particular personal functions that the veteran is unable to perform should be considered in connection with their condition as a whole.  38 C.F.R. § 3.352 (a); see also Turco v. Brown, 9 Vet. App. 222, 224 (1996).  

The January 2021 JMR shows that it was agreed that although a July 2019 VA examiner noted the Veteran's PTSD and addressed his condition, the examiner did not discuss what role the Veteran's stroke played in his cognitive and physical impairment.  As a result, it remains unclear as to how much of the Veteran's need for aid and attendance can be attributed to his service-connected PTSD, or his non-service-connected residuals of a stroke.  

In June 2022, another medical opinion was obtained.  In October 2022, the Board denied the claim.  

The July 2023 JMR shows that it was agreed that the Board's October 2022 decision failed to ensure substantial compliance with the January 2021 JMR, which ordered VA to schedule the Veteran for an aid and attendance/housebound examination to determine if his service-connected PTSD alone resulted in physical and/or mental impairments that  rendered him so helpless as to require the regular aid and attendance of another person or result in his being confined to his house.  The JMR stated that in answering that question, the examiner should address the role that the Veteran's non-service-connected stroke residuals played in his cognitive and physical impairment, and the Veteran's spouse's contention that his PTSD symptoms had intensified after the stroke.  The JMR states that the June 2022 examiner appears to have limited her opinion to whether the Veteran still suffered from PTSD.  

A statement from the Veteran's spouse, received in February 2016, shows that he reports the following: The Veteran had a stroke five years ago, leaving him with paralysis to the right side of his body and speech impairment.  He is house bound.  He needs daily assistance with bathing, feeding, dressing, attending to the wants of nature, and protection from household hazards.   

By way of history, a VA examination for housebound status or permanent need for regular aid and attendance report (VA Form 21-2680) dated in June 2010 showed that the diagnosis was left MCA (middle cerebral artery) stroke with right hemiparesis and fluent and near-fluent aphasia.  This report indicated that the Veteran requires nursing home care due to right hemiparesis.  He cannot feed himself or prepare his own meals.  He requires medication management due to aphasia.  He cannot manage his own financial affairs.  He had 0/5 strength in his right upper extremity, and 5/5 strength in his left upper extremity.  Strength in the bilateral lower extremities was 2/5.  He is generally bed-bound.  Other VA reports dated in 2010 showed that the Veteran was in rehabilitation following a stroke in April 2010.  The findings included cognitive impairment and aphasia.  There was a notation that the Veteran was suffering from an adjustment disorder with anxiety and depression secondary to his stroke.  See October 2010 VA PTSD examination report.  

In July 2012, the RO increased the Veteran's rating for PTSD to 100 percent, citing symptoms that included anxiety, chronic sleep impairment, and depressed mood.  

The evidence dated during the time period in issue includes a May 2016 VA examination for housebound status or permanent need for regular aid and attendance report (VA Form 21-2680) which indicates the following: The Veteran is able to feed himself, but only with his left upper extremity; he cannot use his right upper extremity.  He cannot speak.  He is confined to bed around the clock.  He cannot prepare his own meals.  He is not legally blind and does not require nursing home care.  He requires medication management.  He cannot manage his own financial affairs.  He is wheelchair bound.  He weight-bears with assistance.  He has poor balance.  He cannot leave his home without assistance.  He needs assistance with bathing and tending to other hygiene needs.   

VA progress notes include notations that the Veteran's yes and no responses were inconsistent and incorrect when asked fairly simple questions, suggesting prominent semantic language impairments.  Sentence length was markedly reduced, only 1 or 2 words at a time, and he was unable to follow simple commands.  The diagnoses included cognitive disorder NOS (not otherwise specified).  Follow-up psychiatric care was recommended to monitor his mood and response to antidepressant medications.  The Veteran's medications included venlafaxine for PTSD and depression, which was increased (doubled) in October 2015.  

A July 2019 VA examination for housebound status or permanent need for regular aid and attendance report (VA Form 21-2680) shows the following: The Veteran is not legally blind and does not require nursing home care.  He requires medication management.  He is able to feed himself, but he cannot prepare his own meals.  He needs assistance in bathing and tending to other hygiene needs.  He cannot manage his own benefits payments or to direct someone to do so.  On examination, he was in a wheelchair.  He could not speak or use his right upper extremity.  He needs help with dressing, transfers, and toileting.  He cannot use his right lower extremity well.  He can only stand or leave his home with assistance, and he requires a wheelchair to leave his home.  He has poor cognitive function.  The diagnosis was PTSD.  

A June 2022 VA PTSD DBQ shows that the Veteran's symptoms were noted to include crying spells, anxiety, sleep difficulties, and difficulty in understanding complex commands.  Speech was unable to be assessed, as he only said "no."  Judgment, insight, thought process, and orientation were unable to be assessed.  The diagnosis was PTSD.  

A June 2022 VA examination for housebound status or permanent need for regular aid and attendance report (VA Form 21-2680) includes findings that the Veteran can feed himself.  He has poor balance, and he occasionally chokes.  He cannot prepare his own meals.  He requires assistance for dressing and undressing.  He requires assistance for bathing, grooming, shaving, and toileting.  The diagnosis was status post infarct with right-sided paralysis.  

A June 2022 VA medical opinion from a psychologist shows that the examiner concluded that the Veteran's service-connected PTSD alone is less likely than not results in physical and/or mental impairments that render him so helpless as to require the regular aid and attendance of another person or result in his being confined to his house.  

A February 2024 VA medical opinion shows that the examiner concluded, "It is my opinion that the claimant's service-connected PTSD alone results in physical and/or mental impairments is less than likely than not render him so helpless as to require the regular aid and attendance of another person or result in his generally being confined to his house."    

The Board finds that the criteria for special monthly compensation based on the need for aid and attendance have been met.  The May 2016 VA examination report does not attribute the Veteran's symptoms to any source.  The JMR shows that it was agreed that the July 2019 and June 2022 VA negative opinions lack probative value.  Although another negative VA opinion was obtained in February 2024, the examiner failed to substantially comply with the Board's January 2024 remand.  That remand directed the examiner to explain the reasons for his or her conclusion.  However, the February 2024 examiner, a psychologist, merely summarized the medical evidence and the prior opinions of other health care providers, without providing her own rationale as to why the Veteran's PTSD has not resulted in the need for aid and attendance.  E.g., "The PTSD has not been noted to be the reason for the housebound or bedridden," and "It has been indicated that it is due to physical conditions" (emphasis added).  This opinion therefore lacks probative value.  Neives-Rodriguez v. Peake, 22 Vet. App. 295, 304 (2008).  

Service connection is in effect for PTSD, evaluated as 100 percent disabling under 38 C.F.R. § 4.130, Diagnostic Code (DC) 9411.  As provided for under DC 9411, the Veteran's symptoms are shown to include gross impairment in communication, and an intermittent inability to perform activities of daily living, including maintenance of minimal personal hygiene.  In Mittleider v. West, 11 Vet. App. 181 (1998), the Court of Veterans Appeals (Court) found that when it is not possible to separate the effects of the service-connected disability from a nonservice-connected condition, 38 C.F.R. § 3.102, which requires the Board to employ reasonable doubt, dictates that such signs and symptoms be attributed to the service-connected disability.  Given the lack of probative value of the VA opinions, there is an insufficient basis to dissociate the Veteran's PTSD symptoms from the residuals of his stroke.  The evidence shows that his symptoms include a daily need for medication management. This raises a reasonable doubt as to whether the Veteran requires care or assistance on a regular basis to protect him from the hazards or dangers incident to his daily environment.  Id.  The Board therefore finds that the evidence is sufficient to show that the Veteran is so helpless as a result of service-connected disability that he is in need of the regular aid and attendance of another person due to service-connected disability.  38 C.F.R. § 3.352.   

(Continued on next page) 

The grant of special monthly compensation based on the need for regular aid and attendance effectively renders moot any issue of entitlement to special monthly compensation on the basis of being housebound, since special monthly compensation based on aid and attendance is the higher benefit and payable at a higher rate.  

 

 

MATTHEW W. BLACKWELDER

Veterans Law Judge

Board of Veterans' Appeals

Attorney for the Board	T.S.E., Counsel

title: BVA Decision 25000006: The legacy appeal is dismissed
text:
Citation Nr: 25000006
Decision Date: 01/02/25	Archive Date: 01/02/25

DOCKET NO. 15-41 160A
DATE: January 2, 2025

ORDER

The legacy appeal is dismissed.

FINDING OF FACT

In April 2024, the Veteran died while this appeal was pending before the Board of Veterans' Appeals (Board).

CONCLUSION OF LAW

Due to the death of the Veteran, the criteria for the dismissal of this appeal have been met. 38 U.S.C. § 7104; 38 C.F.R. § 20.1302.

REASONS AND BASES FOR FINDING AND CONCLUSION

The Veteran served honorably in the Army from November 1968 to August 1971.

These matters come before the Board of Veterans' Appeals (Board) on appeal from an October 2012 rating decision by the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) Regional Office (RO) and were previously remanded by the Board in June 2020.  

In February 2020, the Veteran testified at a Board hearing before the undersigned. 

In July 2023, the Board issued a decision which the Veteran subsequently appealed to the United States Court of Appeals for Veteran's Claims (the Court).

Unfortunately, in April 2024, the Veteran died.  

The Board acknowledges that in May 2024, the Veteran's representative submitted a motion to withdraw from representation in this matter. Considering the contents of this motion, the Board finds that the requirements of a withdrawal of representation contained in 38 C.F.R. § 20.6 have not been met and to ensure due process, the representative of record is retained for the purpose of this dismissal.  

In September 2024, the Court issued a decision vacating the appealed Board decision and dismissing the appeal unless there has been a request for substitution in the appeal before the Court. Accordingly, the Court dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction. 

Unfortunately, as the Veteran died during the pendency of the appeal, as a matter of law, the Board cannot issue a decision on the underlying claims at this time and must dismiss this appeal. 38 C.F.R. § 20.1302(a).

The Board's dismissal does not affect the right of an eligible person to take the Veteran's place to continue the appeal on the pending claims. This process, known as substitution, must be requested within one year of the Veteran's death. 38 C.F.R. § 3.1010(a), (b). Individuals who may be eligible for substitution include the Veteran's surviving spouse, dependent children, dependent parents, and those who bore the expenses of last sickness or burial. 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.1000(a), 3.1010(a).

In this case, no one has requested to substitute for the Veteran. Any person who would like to request substitution must submit a VA Form 21P-0847, "Request for Substitution of Claimant Upon Death of Claimant." The form and filing instructions are available online at https://www.va.gov/find-forms/. If the AOJ receives a request for substitution within one year of the Veteran's death and then grants the request, this dismissed appeal will resume its place on the Board's docket. 38 C.F.R. § 20.1302(a).

Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed.

 

 

Nathaniel Doan

Veterans Law Judge

Board of Veterans' Appeals

Attorney for the Board	N. M. Younan

title: BVA Decision 25000007: Entitlement to service connection for gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is granted
text:
Citation Nr: 25000007
Decision Date: 01/02/25	Archive Date: 01/02/25

DOCKET NO. 19-22 400
DATE: January 2, 2025

ORDER

Entitlement to service connection for gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is granted. 

Entitlement to service connection for gastroenteritis is denied.  

FINDINGS OF FACT

1. The Veteran's GERD is due to service.

2. Gastroenteritis is not shown to be causally or etiologically related to any disease, injury, or incident during service.

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

1. The criteria for entitlement to service connection for GERD have been met.  38 U.S.C. §§ 1101, 1110, 1112, 1113, 1116, 1137, 5107; 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.102, 3.303, 3.304, 3.310. 

2. The criteria for service connection for gastroenteritis have not been met.  38 U.S.C. §§ 1101, 1110, 1137, 5107; 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.102, 3.303, 3.307, 3.309.

REASONS AND BASES FOR FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS

The appellant is a Veteran who served on active duty from November 1967 to December 1970 and from April 1973 to October 1992.  This matter is before the Board of Veterans' Appeals (Board) on appeal from a rating decision from the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) Regional Office (RO). 

In March 2022, a Video Conference Board hearing was held before the undersigned.  A transcript of the hearing is associated with the Veteran's claims file.

In October 2023, the Board remanded these claims for additional development.  The requested action has been taken and the case was returned to the Board for adjudication.

Service Connection

Military personnel records confirm service in the Republic of Vietnam and Southwest (SW) Asia during the Persian Gulf War.

Service in Vietnam has been conceded.  In the case of veterans who have been exposed to an herbicide agent during active service, 38 C.F.R. § 3.309(e) generally provides for presumptive service connection for certain listed diseases, which listed diseases do not include dermatitis, gastroenteritis, or GERD.  See also 38 U.S.C. § 1116.  

A veteran may nevertheless prove entitlement to service connection on a direct basis due to herbicide exposure.  See Combee v. Brown, 5 Vet. App. 248 (1993); Stefl v. Nicholson, 21 Vet. App. 120 (2007) (holding that the availability of presumptive service connection for some conditions based on exposure to Agent Orange does not preclude direct service connection for other conditions based on exposure to Agent Orange).  

The Veteran served in the Southwest Asia theater of operations in support of Persian Gulf War.  38 C.F.R. § 3.317(e).  Under those provisions, service connection may be established for objective indications of a chronic disability resulting from an undiagnosed illness or illnesses, provided that such disability (1) became manifest in service on active duty in the Armed Forces in the Southwest Asia theater of operations during the Persian Gulf War; and (2) by history, physical examination, and laboratory tests cannot be attributed to a known clinical diagnosis.  38 U.S.C. § 1117; 38 C.F.R. § 3.317.

At the Board hearing, he reported his service in Vietnam and Saudi Arabia, and related his conditions may be related to either tour.  VA has conceded that the Veteran participated in a Toxic Exposure Risk Activity (TERA) during his military service. 

1. Entitlement to service connection for GERD

In February 1974, the Veteran was noted to have gastroenteritis, with the etiology undetermined.  In April 1975, he had complaints of stomach pain for 3 to 4 days and was noted to have a history of peptic ulcer disease.  In September 1979, he complained of severe stomach pain and discomfort.  He had classic peptic ulcer disease symptoms of epigastric pain.  He reported chronic mid-epigastric pain since 1967.  In November 1979, he was noted to have a peptic ulcer with severe pyloric spasm.  He was noted to have a long history of dyspepsia dating back many years.    

In January 2018, he underwent an esophageal examination.  He reported being diagnosed with GERD during service, however, review of the STRs did not support this contention.  He was diagnosed with peptic ulcer disease during service and had been taking Tagamet for the condition which is also the same medication to treat GERD.  He had an EGD in November 1979 which showed duodenal ulcer, but with no mention of GERD.  The examiner stated there are no objective findings of chronic GERD, and concluded it is less likely as not that the Veteran's current GI complaints were caused by or related to service.  

VAMC records note in September 2018 and March 2019 a diagnosis of GERD, and treatment of famotidine, which he was taking nightly to treat stomach acid.

At the Board hearing he reported experiencing gastrointestinal discomfort during service that has continued to present.  He is in receipt of service connection for a duodenal ulcer.

In January 2023, the Veteran underwent an examination.  The examiner detailed the Veteran's inservice treatment for peptic ulcer disease and a duodenal ulcer, however, the examiner found no indication of GERD during service.  The Veteran had no complaints of heartburn, acid regurgitation, or reflux during service.  The examiner indicated the Veteran had no signs or symptoms due to an esophageal condition, to include GERD; concluding GERD is less likely than not proximately due to or the result of service.  The Veteran is prescribed famotidine which is indicated for the treatment of stomach ulcers, erosive esophagitis, and GERD; however, the records do not show for which pathology famotidine was prescribed.  A UGI in September 1979 was normal, and an EGD in November 1979 showed duodenal ulcer or with no mention of GERD or esophagitis.  Therefore, GERD was less likely than not caused by his duodenal ulcer.  The claimed GERD was less likely than not aggravated beyond natural progression by the duodenal ulcer.  The rationale is there is no pathology consistent with GERD found.  

In a July 2023 addendum, the examiner concluded gastroenteritis and GERD are less likely than not related to service.  The examiner explained there is no current chronic condition of gastroenteritis or GERD found on exam, and the conditions are not known to be caused by herbicide exposure.   

The examiner found that GERD was less likely than not due to an undiagnosed illness or medically unexplained chronic multi-symptom illness resulting from service in SW Asia.  The examiner found that the Veteran does not have GERD and/or gastroenteritis but noted that he is currently taking medications to treat gastrointestinal symptoms.  The examiner did not however, clarify the nature of these gastrointestinal symptoms and whether they could be the result of service in SW Asia.

In a November 2023 opinion, the examiner stated the Veteran does not have an intestinal condition.  He is currently prescribed famotidine, which is indicated for the treatment of stomach ulcers, esophagitis, and GERD.  The records do not show for which pathology famotidine is prescribed.  As to GERD, the examiner stated GERD is a disease with a clear and specific etiology and diagnosis and happens when your lower esophageal sphincter becomes weak or relaxes when it should not, causing stomach contents to rise up into the esophagus.  Therefore, GERD is less likely due to an undiagnosed illness or medically unexplained chronic multi-symptom illness resulting from service in Southwest Asia during the Persian Gulf War.  Further the examiner concluded the Veteran does have a history of GERD as indicated by the January 2023 disability benefits questionnaire.  

In May 2024, the Veteran underwent an examination and was diagnosed with GERD and a duodenal ulcer.  

In a separate May 2024 opinion, the examiner noted the Veteran's medical history and his reports of heartburn, acidic taste in mouth, and nausea, and treatment with Famotidine.  The examiner explained the Veteran has GERD, which is a disease with a clear and specific etiology and diagnosis.  Further, GERD was less likely than not caused by the indicated toxic exposure risk activity.  Additionally, the examiner explained, though there is evidence of an association between GERD and TERA exposure in the medical literature, there is no objective finding to support direct causation.  Outside risk factors, stress and being overweight, would outweigh risks identified by TERA, in which there are none.   

In a September 2024 addendum, the examiner indicated the Veteran did not have GERD. 

In a November 2024 addendum, the examiner indicated the Veteran did have GERD.  The examiner concluded the Veteran's GERD diagnosis is considered chronic gastrointestinal disability of known etiology; therefore, it is not presumed to be due to his Persian Gulf service. 

The Veteran reported symptoms of dyspepsia and epigastric pain during service.  2018 and 20199 VA treatment records confirm a diagnosis of GERD.  He has consistently reported gastrointestinal discomfort since service.  A Veteran is also competent to testify regarding facts or circumstances that can be observed and described by a layperson.  

The May 2024 examining provider noted the Veteran's medical history, the Veteran's diagnosis of GERD, and treatment with Famotidine.  The examiner concluded GERD was less likely than not caused by the indicated toxic exposure risk activity.  The examiner explained there is evidence of an association between GERD and TERA exposure in the medical literature, and noted outside risk factors that would outweigh risks identified by TERA.  After noting the association between GERD and TERA, the examiner found the Veteran has no outside risk factors for the development of GERD.  

There is both positive and negative evidence as to whether the Veteran has a current diagnosis of GERD and there is positive and negative evidence as to whether the Veteran's GERD is related to service (including TERA).  The evidence is nearly balanced as to whether the Veteran has a diagnosis of GERD that is related to service.  Thus, all reasonable doubt is resolved in the Veteran's favor, and service connection for GERD is granted.  

2. Entitlement to service connection for gastroenteritis

In February 1974, the Veteran was noted to have gastroenteritis, with the etiology undetermined.  In April 1975, he had complaints of stomach pain for 3 to 4 days and was noted to have a history of peptic ulcer disease.  In September 1979, he complained of severe stomach pain and discomfort.  He had classic peptic ulcer disease symptoms of epigastric pain.  He reported chronic mid-epigastric pain since 1967.  In November 1979, he was noted to have a peptic ulcer with severe pyloric spasm.  He was noted to have a long history of dyspepsia dating back many years.    

In January 2018, he underwent an esophageal examination.  He was diagnosed with peptic ulcer disease during service and had been taking Tagamet for the condition which is also the same medication to treat GERD.  The examiner stated there are no objective findings of chronic GERD, and concluded it is less likely as not that the Veteran's current GI complaints were caused by or related to service. 

At the Board hearing he reported experiencing gastrointestinal discomfort during service that has continued to present.  He is in receipt of service connection for a duodenal ulcer.

In January 2023, the Veteran underwent an examination.  The examiner explained the Veteran does not have symptoms consistent with gastroenteritis.  The examiner noted that gastroenteritis is typically a short-term infectious illness of the gastrointestinal tract with symptoms of nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and fever.  It can be viral or bacterial and is typically short lived.  The examiner indicated that duodenal ulcer is not known to cause or contribute to the development of gastroenteritis.  During service, he had one episode of acute gastroenteritis.  The Veteran is currently prescribed famotidine.  Famotidine is indicated for the treatment of stomach ulcers, erosive esophagitis, and GERD.  The examiner noted the records do not show for which pathology the Veteran's famotidine is prescribed.  The examiner found no evidence to support a diagnosis of chronic gastroenteritis while the Veteran served active duty, or post-separation.  History or symptoms consistent with gastroenteritis are not noted at the 1992 retirement physical.  Therefore, the examiner concluded that gastroenteritis was less likely than not caused by his duodenal ulcer.  Further, gastroenteritis was less likely than not related to exposure to herbicide agents such as Agent Orange.  

In a July 2023 addendum, the examiner concluded gastroenteritis is less likely than not related to service.  The examiner explained there is no current chronic condition of gastroenteritis found on exam, and the condition is not known to be caused by herbicide exposure.  The examiner found that the Veteran does not have gastroenteritis but noted that he is currently taking medications to treat other gastrointestinal symptoms.  The examiner did not; however, clarify the nature of these gastrointestinal symptoms and whether they could be the result of service in SW Asia.

In a November 2023 opinion, the examiner stated the Veteran does not have an intestinal condition.  The examiner concluded the Veteran does not have symptoms consistent with gastroenteritis.  Records show the Veteran had one occasion of gastroenteritis during service.  He is currently prescribed famotidine, which is indicated for the treatment of stomach ulcers, esophagitis, and GERD.  The records do not show for which pathology famotidine is prescribed.  Gastroenteritis was less likely than not related to an event, injury, or disease in active duty.  The examiner concluded the claimed condition was less likely than not caused by the indicated toxic exposure risk activities, after considering the total potential exposure through all applicable military deployments of the Veteran and the synergistic, combined effect of all toxic exposure risk activities of the Veteran.  There is no pathology to warrant a diagnosis that can be related to the claimed toxic exposure.  To conclude, the claimed condition of gastroenteritis is less likely than not related to an event injury or disease in service.  The examiner concluded there is no functional gastrointestinal disorder pathology or condition, and he does not have gastroenteritis.  

In May 2024, the Veteran underwent an examination and the examiner concluded there is no evidence of gastroenteritis, or a gastrointestinal disorder.  The examiner stated there is no pathology to warrant a diagnosis or condition that can be related to the claimed condition of gastroenteritis.  

In a separate May 2024 opinion, the examiner noted the Veteran's medical history and concluded the Veteran does not have a diagnosis of gastroenteritis.  He reported a history of heartburn, acidic taste in mouth, and nausea, and treats with Famotidine.  The examiner explained the Veteran has GERD, which is a disease with a clear and specific etiology and diagnosis. 

Given the overwhelming evidence of record, the evidence does not indicate the Veteran has a diagnosis of gastroenteritis during the appeal period.  The Veteran had an acute and transitory episode of gastroenteritis during service, that did not persist post-service.  The January 2023 examiner found the Veteran does not have symptoms consistent with gastroenteritis and noted the Veteran's acute and transitory episode of gastroenteritis during service.  Thus, the January 2023 examiner found, there is no direct link to service, or to exposure to herbicide agents.  

As for the claim of a nexus to his SW Asia service, although he served during the Persian Gulf War, he cannot establish service connection for an undiagnosed illness under 38 C.F.R. § 3.317, because there is no indication of a chronic disability as to a gastrointestinal disorder that manifests as gastroenteritis.  As was found by the November 2023 examiner, the Veteran does not have symptoms consistent with gastroenteritis, and concluded the claimed condition was less likely than not caused by a TERA activity.  There is no pathology to warrant a diagnosis that can be related to the claimed toxic exposure. 

The Board considered the Veteran's reports regarding his gastrointestinal symptoms, which he is competent to report.  However, the Board finds the persuasive evidence is against the Veteran's claim for service connection for gastroenteritis, or a functional gastrointestinal condition.  Although the Veteran believes he suffers from gastroenteritis symptoms that are related to an in-service injury, he is not competent to provide a nexus opinion in this case.  The record does not reflect that he has the requisite training or expertise to offer a medical opinion diagnosing a gastrointestinal condition and linking his current symptoms to an in-service injury and as such he is not competent to provide an opinion in this case.  Jandreau v. Nicholson, 492 F.3d 1372, 1377 (Fed. Cir. 2007).

The medical evidence is more probative and more credible than the lay opinions of record.  The January 2023 and November 2023 VA examination did not find any indication of a gastrointestinal disorder on examination with the exception of the diagnosis of GERD.  Further, the treatment records are absent for an indication of a gastroenteritis.  Thus, the more persuasive evidence of record indicates the Veteran does not have gastroenteritis or a functional gastrointestinal disorder, to include as due to service in Vietnam and/or SW Asia, and service connection is not warranted.

(Continued on the next page)

?

As such, the Board finds that service connection for gastroenteritis is not warranted.  As the persuasive evidence is against the claim, the benefit of the doubt rule is not applicable.  For these reasons, the claim is denied.

 

 

H.M. WALKER

Veterans Law Judge

Board of Veterans' Appeals

Attorney for the Board	Skiouris, Elena

The Board's decision in this case is binding only with respect to the instant matter decided. This decision is not precedential and does not establish VA policies or interpretations of general applicability. 38 C.F.R. § 20.1303.

title: BVA Decision 25000008
text:
Citation Nr: 25000008
Decision Date: 01/02/25	Archive Date: 01/02/25

DOCKET NO. 18-04 499
DATE: January 2, 2025

REMANDED

The claim of entitlement to service connection for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is remanded.

REASONS FOR REMAND

The Veteran served on active duty from March 1963 to March 1965.

This matter comes to the Board of Veterans' Appeals (Board) on appeal of a rating decision by a Regional Office (RO) of the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA).

The claim is remanded. 

This case has been subject to multiple actions by the Board and by the U.S. Court of Appeal for Veterans Claims (Court). Most recently, in September 2024, the Board remanded the matter for additional medical inquiry pursuant to a Court remand in August 2023.

Unfortunately, an additional remand is needed. The United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims (Court) has held that a permanent worsening of a non-service-connected disability is not required to establish secondary service connection on the basis of aggravation (i.e., aggravation may include temporary worsening of a disability).  See Ward v. Wilkie, 31 Vet. App. 233, 239-40 (2019).  The prior Board remand requested a secondary opinion as to the Veteran's COPD disorder as secondary to his service-connected lung cancer. 

The responding opinion for aggravation addresses why the Veteran's COPD has not been permanently aggravated by his lung cancer.  However, the opinion also suggests that the Veteran's COPD was temporarily aggravated by his lung cancer. Specifically, the opinion indicates that the Veteran "developed pneumothorax during resection of his lung cancer in 2016."  While the opinion indicates that the pneumothorax resolved, it does not explain why this was not a temporary worsening of his COPD due to his lung cancer. 

As whether or not aggravation, temporary or permanent worsening, has occurred was part of the Board's prior remand directives, a remand is needed to ensure adequate compliance.  See Stegall v. West, 11 Vet. App. 268, 271 (1998) (holding veterans are entitled to compliance with Board remand instructions). 

The Board acknowledges the Sergeant First Class Heath Robinson Honoring our Promise to Address Comprehensive Toxics Act of 2022 (PACT Act) provides that a TERA medical examination/opinion is required in cases of toxic-exposed veterans where there is a claim for a disability that is not clearly due to an etiology not associated with toxic exposure (such as in cases of physical trauma or mental disorders), and the evidence is not otherwise sufficient to establish service connection for the disability.  See 38 U.S.C. §§ 101 (38); 1168(a), 1710(e)(1)., Pub. L. 117-168, § 303 (to be codified at 38 U.S.C. § 1168).  Yet, the Secretary of VA has determined that there is no positive association between exposure to herbicide agents and COPD.  See VBA Letter 20-22-10, Processing Claims Involving the PACT Act, 87 Fed. Reg. 78,543 (Dec. 22, 2022) (detailing the four situations in which VA currently finds no indication of an association between the claimed disability and a TERA).  As such, the Board finds that a VA examination for toxic exposure risk activity on the basis of herbicide exposure is not warranted. 

However, the Veteran has also asserted toxic exposures to asbestos insulation.  As a result, the Board infers from the Veteran's claim that he has raised the issue of a toxic exposure risk activity (TERA) with respect to asbestos. The sub-regulatory guidance to the PACT Act states that both explicit and implicit claims include claims related to garrison exposures, which are any environmental exposure experienced while stationed on a military base including asbestos.  Accordingly, the Board finds that a TERA opinion is required as provided for under the PACT Act for the Veteran's COPD. 

The matters are REMANDED for the following action:

1. In rendering the requested opinion, the examiner must address and consider (1) the total potential toxic exposure through the Veteran's military deployment and (2) the synergistic, combined effect of all toxic exposure risk activities of the Veteran.

2. Return the case to VA examiner who issued the October 2024 VA reports, or to a suitable substitute, for issuance of an addendum medical opinion.  After reviewing the claims file, the examiner should address the following question(s):

(a.) Opine as to whether it is at least as likely as not (i.e. a 50 percent or greater probability) that the Veteran's COPD had its onset during, or is otherwise related to, his active-duty service, to include claimed asbestos exposure?

In rendering the requested opinion, the examiner must address and consider (1) the total potential toxic exposure through the Veteran's military deployment and (2) the synergistic, combined effect of all toxic exposure risk activities of the Veteran.

(b.) Is it approximately at least as likely as not that COPD has been aggravated (i.e., temporarily or permanently worsened) by service-connected lung cancer?

The evidentiary standard "at least as likely as not" is defined as the "likelihood is at least approximately balanced or nearly equal, if not higher." Conversely, "less likely than not" is defined as the "likelihood is less than approximately balanced or nearly equal."

In rendering the requested opinions, the examiner should note that the Veteran is competent to attest to matters of which he has first-hand knowledge, including observable symptomatology.

In remanding this case, the Board makes no credibility determination, expressed or implied, at this juncture.

(Continued on the next page)

?

Please explain in detail any opinion provided and the supporting rationale.

If the examiner cannot provide an opinion without resorting to mere speculation, he or she shall provide a complete explanation for why an opinion cannot be rendered.  In so doing, the examiner shall explain whether the inability to provide a more definitive opinion is the result of a need for additional information, or that he or she has exhausted the limits of current medical knowledge in providing an answer to that particular question(s).

 

 

G. A. WASIK

Veterans Law Judge

Board of Veterans' Appeals

Attorney for the Board	J. Wade, Counsel

title: BVA Decision 25000009
text:
Citation Nr: 25000009
Decision Date: 01/02/25	Archive Date: 01/02/25

DOCKET NO. 18-13 806
DATE: January 2, 2025

REMANDED

Entitlement to service connection for an acquired psychiatric disorder, to include post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), is remanded. 

Entitlement to a total disability rating based on individual unemployability (TDIU) is remanded. 

REASONS FOR REMAND

The Veteran served on active duty in the United States Army from April 1969 to November 1970. These matters return to the Board of Veterans' Appeals (Board) after they were remanded by the Board in December 2023. 

Although the Board sincerely regrets the additional delay, these matters must be remanded once again for additional development.

Entitlement to service connection for an acquired psychiatric disorder, to include PTSD.

In its December 2023 remand, the Board directed the Agency of Original Jurisdiction (AOJ) to schedule the Veteran for a VA examination to determine whether the Veteran suffers from a psychiatric disability due to his active-duty service. The remand specified that the examiner must specifically address the Veteran's July 2022 positive screening for PTSD.

Following a May 2024 VA examination, the examiner concluded that the Veteran did not suffer from PTSD or any other mental disability. In doing so, he acknowledged that the Veteran experienced various stressors, including witnessing shells firing overhead and artillery fire, and firing his weapon. However, he did not at all address the Veteran's July 2022 positive screen for PTSD nor did he indicate that the Veteran suffered from any mental health symptoms at all. Indeed, he left the entire lengthy list of mental health symptomatology unchecked. 

VA's duty to assist a veteran in substantiating his claim includes obtaining a medical examination when necessary and ensuring that it is adequate to decide the claim. See 38?U.S.C. §?5103A(d); see Barr v Nicholson, 21?Vet. App.?303, 312 (2007). An examination report is inadequate if it provides an incomplete analysis or if it does not consider all the relevant evidence of record. Stefl v. Nicholson, 21?Vet. App.?120 (2007); Nieves-Rodriquez v. Peake, 22?Vet. App.?295 (2008); Dalton v. Nicholson, 21?Vet. App.?23 (2007).

As the May 2024 examiner failed to provide an appropriate explanation for failing to diagnose the Veteran with any psychiatric disability, a remand is required.

Entitlement to a TDIU is remanded. 

On the same basis, this matter must also be remanded. Pursuant to the Board's remand, an Individual Unemployability statement was prepared in March 2024. However, it concluded, without any explanation whatsoever, that the Veteran is capable of performing sedentary work. It did not discuss what service-connected disabilities are implicated in the Veteran's employment limitations nor did it provide any rationale as to why sedentary work is possible, while physical work is not. 

A concurrent VA examination indicates that the Veteran's diabetes mellitus, type II, prevents him from doing strenuous work and that the Veteran is easily fatigued with pain, numbness and tingling. Also, he cannot walk or stand for long periods of time. This is consistent with a conclusion that the Veteran can nevertheless do sedentary work. 

However, another examination report indicates that the Veteran's bilateral upper and lower diabetic peripheral neuropathy has a "profound" impact on his work due to pain, tingling and numbness; and that it hinders the Veteran's physical ability but also his fine motor skills and coordination, potentially impacting activities that require precision and dexterity. It stands to reason that this would significantly limit the Veteran's ability to complete sedentary work.

Based on this, the Board finds that a remand is required for an addendum opinion that specifically addresses the impact of the Veteran's bilateral upper and lower peripheral neuropathy on his ability to do sedentary work.

The matters are REMANDED for the following action:

1. Schedule the Veteran for a psychiatric examination with a new examiner to determine the nature and etiology of any PTSD. The examiner must consider and specifically address the Veteran's July 2022 positive screening for PTSD. If the Veteran is diagnosed with PTSD, the examiner must explain how the diagnostic criteria are met and opine whether it is at least as likely as not related to a verified in-service stressor. 

If any other acquired psychiatric disorders are diagnosed, the examiner must opine whether each diagnosed disorder is at least as likely as not related to an in-service injury, event, or disease. 

2. Afterward, obtain a new Individual Unemployability statement that discusses the impact of all of the Veteran's service-connected disabilities and that specifically addresses whether and how the Veteran's upper and lower bilateral peripheral neuropathy affects his ability to participate in sedentary work. 

 

Wendy Daknis

Veterans Law Judge

Board of Veterans' Appeals

Attorney for the Board	Freda J. F. Smith, Counsel
